title: The Day of Atonement
lead: The yearly day when the high priest entered the most holy place with blood to cleanse the sanctuary and the people (Leviticus 16; 23:26–32). Its center was the kapporet, the atonement lid of the ark. Jews keep it as Yom Kippur, a day of fasting and repentance; Hebrews 9 reads it as fulfilled in Christ.

sections.b: Leviticus 16 sets out the rite. Once a year, on the tenth of the seventh month, the high priest puts aside his splendid clothes for plain linen, offers a bull for himself and his household, and enters the most holy place behind a cloud of incense to sprinkle blood on and before the atonement lid. Two goats are chosen by lot: one is offered as a sin offering for the people, and the blood cleanses the sanctuary, altar and tent from Israel's impurities; on the other, the scapegoat, he confesses the people's sins and sends it into the desert "to Azazel." The people fast and do no work (Leviticus 16:29–31; 23:26–32; Numbers 29:7–11). The Mishnah tractate Yoma describes the Second Temple practice, and Hebrews 9:7–14 reads the day as fulfilled in Christ.
